interviewQuestions.question: Explain matrix factorization for recommendations to a non-ML interviewer.
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
I'd open with the matrix itself: picture a giant spreadsheet, users down the rows, movies across the columns, and a rating in each cell where a user actually rated that movie — which is almost none of them. The goal is filling in the blanks.

The idea: imagine we could describe every user and every movie using the same handful of hidden 'taste dimensions' — how much action, how much romance, how arthouse. If we had those numbers for every user and every movie, predicting a rating is just checking how well a user's taste profile lines up with a movie's profile. The trick is we never hand-design those dimensions — we let an algorithm discover whatever handful of dimensions best reconstructs the ratings we already have, then those same discovered dimensions let us predict the ratings we don't.

Concretely: this is exactly how the 2006 Netflix Prize was mostly won — teams factorized the ratings matrix into user and movie latent vectors and multiplied them back together to fill in the blanks.

**Testing:** whether you can compress a linear-algebra technique into an intuitive, jargon-free story — a core skill for explaining ML decisions to non-technical stakeholders.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Explaining matrix factorization simply

interviewQuestions.question: Why does matrix factorization handle sparsity so much better than user-based or item-based neighborhood methods?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
Neighborhood methods depend on direct overlap: to say two users are similar, user-based CF needs them to have both rated some of the same items, and the similarity computation only uses that shared overlap. In a typical catalog where a user has interacted with well under 1% of items, most pairs of users share only a handful of common ratings — or none at all — which makes the computed similarity either statistically unreliable (two users who happen to share only 2 overlapping ratings can look artificially near-identical from pure noise) or simply undefined (zero overlap means no basis for comparison whatsoever). The sparser the matrix, the less direct overlap exists to compute from, and neighborhood methods have no way to route around that — they're fundamentally built on pairwise overlap.

Matrix factorization sidesteps this because it doesn't require any two users or items to have direct overlap at all. Every user and item is mapped into the same shared latent space, learned jointly across the *entire* matrix at once — so a user's latent vector is informed by every rating they've given, and it can end up close to another user's latent vector purely because both vectors were shaped by similar patterns propagating through the shared item-factor structure, even if the two users never rated a single common item. This is sometimes described as similarity through a chain of shared latent structure: user A and user B might never overlap directly, but both might be similar to user C who links them transitively through the learned factors, and the model captures that without ever needing to compute an explicit A-B comparison.

The practical consequence: matrix factorization can make reasonable predictions for a user with very few ratings, as long as the *overall* matrix has enough density for the latent factors to be well-estimated, whereas neighborhood methods degrade sharply exactly where sparsity is worst.

**Testing:** whether you can explain the mechanism (joint latent space vs pairwise overlap) rather than just asserting matrix factorization handles sparsity better as received wisdom.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Why matrix factorization is more sparsity-robust

interviewQuestions.question: Your recommender is trained on implicit feedback (clicks, watches) rather than explicit ratings. Why can't you treat 'never interacted with this item' the same way you'd treat a 1-star rating?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
The core problem is that implicit feedback has no true negatives — only positives and unknowns — and conflating "unknown" with "negative" builds in a systematic bias that a genuine low rating doesn't have. A 1-star explicit rating is unambiguous: the user saw the item and actively disliked it. "Never watched this show" carries none of that certainty — it could mean the user would dislike it, or it could simply mean they haven't discovered it yet, haven't had time, or don't know it exists. Treating every unobserved interaction as an explicit strong negative would train the model to actively suppress items a user might genuinely love, purely because they haven't gotten around to them yet — which is close to the opposite of what a recommender should do.

The standard fix, used in implicit-feedback matrix factorization approaches like weighted ALS, reframes the entire objective rather than trying to force implicit data into an explicit-ratings shape: treat every unobserved interaction as a *weak* negative (not a confident one) and every observed interaction as a *positive*, then weight the loss by confidence rather than treating all signals equally. A video watched ten times is a much more confident positive signal than one watched once, so it gets weighted more heavily in the loss; an item never interacted with contributes a very weak negative signal, acknowledging real uncertainty about whether it's actually disliked or just unseen.

This changes what the model is actually solving: not "predict this user's rating for this item" (which implicit data can't really support, since there's no rating), but "predict the confidence that this user prefers this item over items they haven't shown any signal on" — a subtly different and more honest framing of what the data actually tells you.

**Testing:** whether you understand why the absence of negatives is the core problem, and can name the confidence-weighting fix rather than treating implicit and explicit feedback as interchangeable.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Why implicit feedback needs a different objective
